intro: Take your seat in the Great Theatre of Ephesus, a building whose story runs from the 3rd century BC to the 2nd century AD. It is one of the largest theatres of antiquity: a three-tiered cavea cut into the slope of Mount Pion, looking down the Harbour Street at a Roman stage building. And it was here, on these very tiers, that the riot of the silversmiths in the Acts of the Apostles took place.
spot-1: Now you are looking down at the orchestra, 26 metres across. In the 3rd century it was walled round and turned into an arena, and the circle that once served the stage took on a new role.
spot-2: Now you are looking at the stage building. Under Nero it was built two storeys high; the third storey was added in the 2nd century. Picture it rising, generation by generation, behind the players.
spot-3: Your eye now follows the first walkway, the one that runs between the lower and middle tiers. Count the seats beneath it: the lower tier alone has 24 rows.
spot-4: Look a little higher and you reach the second walkway. It separates the middle tier from the upper one, a tier that was added in the 1st century.
spot-5: Now you are looking at the whole three-tiered cavea: 24, 22 and 21 rows, 67 in all. It is usually said to have seated about 24,000 people, though some estimates give 21,500. Pause for a moment and imagine every one of those seats filled.
spot-6: And now the camera rises to the upper gallery, the covered passage behind the top row, at the crest of the slope. From up here the whole bowl opens out beneath you.
uncertainty: Finally, an honest word about what this model does not know. The diameter of the cavea and the orchestra, and the row counts of the three tiers, come from the archive record; the seat tread (0.7 m), the riser and the width of the two walkways are derived to fit them into 142 metres. The three-storey stage front is not measured. It is proportioned to 18 metres from the record that it was built two storeys high under Nero and given its third in the 2nd century, and its doorways and aediculae follow a generic Roman stage wall, as at Aspendos, rather than copying the one at Ephesus. The 3rd-century conversion of the orchestra into an arena, the exact stairway count and the awning masts are not modelled.
